title: Cerebrospinal Fluid Shunt and Drain Infections

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man presented with a fever of 39°C and disorientation. He had a history of myelomeningocele and a ventriculoperitoneal shunt. He had no drug allergies. Investigations: Head CT scan: consistent with ventriculitis CSF microscopy: 250 nucleated cells with 85% neutrophils CSF glucose 25 mg/dL CSF protein 110 mg/dL CSF culture positive for Proteus mirabilis, sensitivities consistent with extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) production
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Meropenem While cefotetan, a cephamycin, is active against many ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae, it is not established for central nervous system infections and is vulnerable to treatment-emergent resistance with these strains. Ceftriaxone is not considered reliably active against ESBL-producing organisms. Gentamicin IV poorly penetrates the central nervous system and is not appropriate for monotherapy of central nervous system infections. Imipenem is reliably active against most ESBL-producing strains but is relatively inactive against Proteus mirabilis and should be avoided for treatment of serious infections caused by this organism. Imipenem is also widely believed to be the most epileptogenic carbapenem, which could be a concern in this case. Meropenem is active against ESBL-producing strains and is clinically established for treatment of central nervous system infections.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q4

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Headache. (2) Nausea/lethargy with change in mental status (from shunt malfunction; seen in up to 65%). (3) Fever (14-92%). (4) Abdominal pain/signs of peritonitis at the distal (peritoneal) shunt terminus.
b) (1) Retrograde infection from the distal end (e.g., peritonitis/bowel perforation) - rare. (2) Through the skin (needle access to reservoir, injection, or breakdown/ulceration of overlying skin). (3) Hematogenous seeding (especially ventriculoatrial shunts). (4) Colonization of the shunt at the time of surgery - the most frequent mechanism.
c) (1) IV vancomycin plus cefepime (or ceftazidime). (2) IV vancomycin plus meropenem.
d) (1) Coagulase-negative staphylococci, especially Staphylococcus epidermidis (47-64%). (2) Staphylococcus aureus (12-29%).
e) Surgical removal of all infected shunt components with placement of an external ventricular drain, continuing systemic antimicrobials, then reimplantation once CSF cultures are negative (two-stage replacement; success >85%).

b) (1) Retrograde infection from the distal (peritoneal) end - rare. (2) Through the skin (reservoir puncture/injection, or breakdown of overlying skin). (3) Hematogenous seeding (especially ventriculoatrial shunts). (4) Colonization at the time of surgery - most frequent.

cohort_answer.text: Symptoms: can be subtle (common pathogens CoNS/C. acnes elicit minimal inflammation), onset may be insidious; headache, change in LOC, nausea, lethargy (often shunt malfunction with infection); fever (14-92%); pain at peritoneal/pleural ends; pain at proximal end (meningitis/ventriculitis). Mechanisms: retrograde infection from distal end via peritonitis (rare); via skin (direct access for sampling/drug infusion, skin breakdown over shunt or failure to heal); hematogenous seeding (especially ventriculoatrial shunts); colonization at time of surgery (MOST COMMON). Empiric: Ceftazidime/vancomycin, Meropenem/vancomycin, Cefepime/vancomycin (healthcare associated). Pathogens: CoNS (S. epidermidis) > S. aureus (staphylococci together 55-95%) > Enterobacteriaceae (6-20%) > Streptococci (8-10%) > diphtheroids (1-14%) > anaerobes (6%) > yeast.

questions.question: Name the typical organisms infecting in the following scenarios.
questions.question_raw: What are the typical organisms infecting in the following scenarios.

parts.text: Cochlear implants.
Laceration that occurs in a lake.
Rat bite in a child who now has fever and rash.
A person competing in a triathlon in South America has fever, high liver enzymes, and conjunctival suffusion.

parts_raw.text: Cochlear implants.

Rat bite in a child who now has fever and rash
Guy competing in a triathlon in South America has fever, high LFTs and conjunctival suffusion

questions.model_answer: a) Streptococcus pneumoniae (leading cause of cochlear implant-associated meningitis; also Haemophilus influenzae). b) Aeromonas hydrophila (also Pseudomonas aeruginosa; freshwater exposure). c) Streptobacillus moniliformis (rat-bite fever; Spirillum minus in Asia). d) Leptospira species (leptospirosis) — fever, elevated LFTs, and conjunctival suffusion after freshwater exposure.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the rat-bite (part c) organism is from this chapter; cochlear implant, freshwater laceration, and leptospirosis organisms are from established Mandell/IDSA knowledge in other chapters.

cohort_answer.text: Cochlear implants: meningitis most commonly S. pneumoniae, less often H. influenzae; localized wound infection most commonly S. aureus (also CoNS, streptococci, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Achromobacter xylosoxidans, Candida albicans); mastoiditis most commonly S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes, S. aureus, Pseudomonas spp, H. influenzae. Lake laceration (fresh/brackish water): Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Aeromonas hydrophila, Chromobacterium violaceum (immunosuppression/CGD), Mycobacterium fortuitum, Plesiomonas shigelloides, Edwardsiella tarda, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Streptococcus iniae (fish preparation); salt water: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae (fish preparation), Mycobacterium marinum, Shewanella spp, Vibrio vulnificus. Rat bite: Streptobacillus moniliformis (most US cases); Spirillum minus (Asia). Triathlon South America: Leptospirosis - abrupt fever, rigors, myalgias, headache after incubation 2-26 days (average 10); conjunctival suffusion important but often overlooked sign (~55% of patients), uncommon in other diseases; subconjunctival hemorrhages also occur.
